slides.title: Any police station
slides.body: For a cognizable offence, any police station must record your FIR, wherever the crime happened. It is then sent to the right station.

slides.title: Free copy, e-FIR too
slides.body: You get a copy of the FIR free of cost. You can also report electronically; sign it at the station within 3 days.

slides.title: If police refuse
slides.body: Send the complaint in writing, by post, to the Superintendent of Police. If arrested, you must see a Magistrate within 24 hours.

caption_instagram:
Told "this is not our area" at the police station? Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, that is not a reason to turn you away. 🚓

📍 Zero FIR: for a cognizable offence, you can give information at any police station, wherever the crime happened; it is transferred to the right station
📄 You get a copy of your FIR free of cost
💻 e-FIR: you can report electronically; sign it at the station within 3 days
✉️ Police refused? Send the substance of your complaint in writing, by post, to the Superintendent of Police (s.173(4))
⚖️ If arrested: you must be told the grounds, can consult a lawyer, and must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Article 22)
🆘 Emergency? Dial 112

caption_linkedin:
Many people are still turned away from police stations with "this is not our jurisdiction." Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 addresses this directly:

• Information about a cognizable offence may be given at any police station, irrespective of where the offence was committed (Zero FIR); it is then transferred to the station with jurisdiction
• Information can be given orally or electronically; an e-FIR is taken on record once the informant signs it within three days
• The informant receives a copy of the FIR free of cost
• If the officer in charge refuses to record it, the substance can be sent in writing and by post to the Superintendent of Police (s.173(4))
• Article 22 of the Constitution guarantees an arrested person the right to know the grounds of arrest, to consult a legal practitioner, and to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours
